title: 1.2 proposal: Function Object and functionId step target (MCP tools, CLI commands, and other calls with no source description)

raw.title: 1.2 proposal: Function Object and functionId step target (MCP tools, CLI commands, and other calls with no source description)
raw.body:
Splitting this out of #410 so function calling can be discussed on its own. It is written so a tool vendor can implement it from this text alone, and it is long because it tries to answer the questions reviewers will ask anyway: what is portable, what is environmental, what happens when an executor cannot run a binding, and how two independent implementations end up making identical decisions.

## The problem

Every step target Arazzo has today resolves to something already described somewhere: `operationId`, `operationPath`, and `channelPath` point into an OpenAPI or AsyncAPI source description, and `workflowId` points at another workflow, in the same document or in an `arazzo` source description.

Real workflows also need to call things that have no such description:

- MCP tools. MCP servers expose tools with JSON Schema contracts, but MCP tools are not necessarily described by OpenAPI or AsyncAPI. No step target can reach one today.
- Command line tools. Plenty of workflows have a step in the middle that is "run this program with these arguments and use its output", usually between two API calls.
- Small deterministic transforms. Reshape a payload, derive a value, normalize a date. Today you either round-trip through an external API that happens to do the transform or you leave the workflow incomplete.
- WebAssembly. Wasm keeps growing as a portable unit of computation, and it has the same shape as everything above: a callable thing with typed input and output and no OpenAPI description.

What people do instead: write a fake OpenAPI document that fronts a non-HTTP thing through a local shim, or hang `x-` extensions off steps. Both work, and both mean every runtime invents its own convention, with no portable contract independent Arazzo tooling can validate.

## The proposal in one paragraph

Add a top-level `functions` section, a sibling of `workflows`: a list of Function Objects, each identified by a required `functionId` the same way workflows are identified by `workflowId`. A Function Object is a portable contract (input and output schemas plus optional behavioral annotations) together with a required, ordered list of bindings, where each binding describes one concrete way to invoke the function. Steps reference a function with `functionId` and pass an `arguments` object. The contract travels with the document and every tool can validate it. Bindings are typed by profile; this issue defines one standard profile, MCP over Streamable HTTP, plus the machinery any future profile plugs into. An executor selects exactly one binding per function before anything runs, deterministically, and never falls back to a different binding at runtime.

Rule zero, the bar everything below serves: two independent implementations, given the same document and equivalent support and policy, make identical decisions at every observable point. Same validation verdict, same selected binding, same error classification for the same failure. Four rules follow from it:

1. The contract is portable, the invocation is environmental. Schemas and annotations mean the same thing everywhere. Whether a binding can run depends on where you are.
2. Nothing in the document grants authority. A binding is a claim about how a function can be invoked, never permission to invoke it.
3. Selection is deterministic and happens before execution. Two conforming executors with the same support and policy select the same binding. There is no runtime fallback.
4. Failure is closed and early. If a referenced function has no eligible binding, preparation fails before the first step executes, not at step 7 of 12.

## Example

```yaml
arazzo: 1.2.0
info:
  title: Ticket triage
  version: 1.0.0
functions:
  - functionId: resolveUser
    summary: Resolve a directory user from a free-form name
    inputSchema:
      type: object
      required: [query]
      properties:
        query: {type: string}
      additionalProperties: false
    outputSchema:
      type: object
      required: [userId]
      properties:
        userId: {type: string}
        displayName: {type: string}
    annotations:
      readOnlyHint: true
      idempotentHint: true
    bindings:
      - bindingId: directoryPrimary
        type: mcp
        serverName: corporate-directory
        tool: resolve_user
      - bindingId: directoryAlternate
        type: mcp
        url: https://directory.example.com/mcp
        tool: resolve_user
workflows:
  - workflowId: triageTicket
    inputs:
      type: object
      properties:
        reporterName: {type: string}
    steps:
      - stepId: who
        functionId: resolveUser
        arguments:
          query: $inputs.reporterName
        successCriteria:
          - condition: $result#/userId != null
        outputs:
          userId: $result#/userId
    outputs:
      userId: $steps.who.outputs.userId
```

The two bindings are the same profile on purpose: the first names a symbolic server the environment resolves from its own configuration, the second names an explicit endpoint. An executor that has no `corporate-directory` configured skips the first and selects the second, before anything runs. That is the whole selection model in one card.

Two more things to notice.

There is no `sourceDescriptions` section. The spec currently requires at least one entry, and a document whose steps are all function calls has nothing to put there. Part of this proposal: `sourceDescriptions` becomes optional in 1.2; when present it MUST still be non-empty, and a document containing steps that target operations or channels MUST include it (that mismatch is a static document error). Authors should omit the section rather than write `[]`.

That requirement was never arbitrary, which is why relaxing it is safe to do now and was not before. Every executable workflow in 1.1 has to bottom out in operation steps somewhere, and operations need source descriptions. Functions are the first leaf-level call that does not. The change is also the permissive direction, so it does not force a major version: every valid 1.0 or 1.1 document already carries the section and remains valid with unchanged meaning, and documents declaring those versions keep the old rule. There is direct precedent one shelf over: OpenAPI 3.1 made the top-level `paths` field optional in a minor release when `webhooks` arrived, because a webhooks-only document was suddenly meaningful. Same shape as this change, and `workflows` stays REQUIRED here, so there is no degenerate empty document to worry about.

The step declares its outputs explicitly (`userId: $result#/userId`). Nothing is inferred from `outputSchema`. I considered implicit outputs and dropped the idea: output schemas can use `$ref`, composition, or non-object roots, and synthesizing outputs from schema properties is exactly the kind of quiet magic that makes two tools disagree.

## Schema details

### Function Object (top-level `functions`)

Functions sit beside `workflows`, not inside `components`, because they are call targets rather than reusable fragments. Every existing step target resolves to something outside `components`, and a step naming a top-level definition by its id is exactly the `workflowId` pattern. `components` members are reached through `$components` expressions; making a step target point into `components` would be the one exception to both conventions. The section is optional; when present it MUST contain at least one Function Object.

| Field | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `functionId` | string | REQUIRED. Case-sensitive; unique among the document's Function Objects (a separate namespace from `workflowId`) |
| `summary` | string | optional |
| `description` | string | optional, CommonMark |
| `inputSchema` | JSON Schema | REQUIRED. Draft 2020-12. Applied to the evaluated `arguments` object |
| `outputSchema` | JSON Schema | REQUIRED. Draft 2020-12. Applied to the normalized result |
| `annotations` | object | optional behavioral hints, below |
| `bindings` | [Binding Object] | REQUIRED, at least one |

On schemas: `inputSchema` and `outputSchema` are full JSON Schema draft 2020-12 schemas, which includes boolean schemas, `$ref`, and composition. The spec does not require the schema to be provably object-shaped, because that is not decidable for arbitrary schemas. Instead: the evaluated arguments are always assembled into a single JSON object and `inputSchema` is applied to that object. Authors SHOULD declare `type: object` at the root so the intent is visible.

Schema scoping, so two tools dereference identically: each schema is a self-contained schema resource. `$ref` resolves within that schema only (via `$defs` and anchors); references into the host Arazzo document or to external URIs are not permitted in 1.2 (a natural later extension, deferred). The dialect is fixed at 2020-12; an embedded `$schema` MUST NOT declare a different one, and a schema that is not structurally valid 2020-12 makes the document invalid.

On bindings being required: I went back and forth on whether a Function could carry a contract and no bindings, with resolution left entirely to the environment, and landed hard on no.

> `bindings` is REQUIRED and MUST contain at least one Function Binding Object. Each binding MUST identify its invocation profile through its required `type`. A binding MAY contain profile-defined symbolic targets that are resolved from implementation configuration during execution preparation.
>
> A Function Object is a semantically self-describing callable definition, not an abstract interface declaration. Implementations MUST NOT infer or synthesize a missing binding from the function's `functionId`, the document URI, or unspecified implementation configuration.

A bindingless function would keep the schemas but lose the profile, and the profile is where serialization, result normalization, cancellation, and error mapping live. Resolving all of that out-of-band means every environment invents a convention, which is the situation this proposal exists to end. Deployment flexibility comes from symbolic targets instead: `serverName: corporate-directory` says how (MCP, that tool) without hard-coding where.

One limitation stated up front: when a function carries multiple bindings, the author is asserting they implement the same logical callable contract. Each must satisfy the same schemas, but schema conformance cannot prove behavioral equivalence. That is an authoring responsibility, the same way `successCriteria` already encode assumptions about behavior.

### Annotations

`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, `idempotentHint`, `openWorldHint`. All boolean, all optional. The vocabulary is field-compatible with MCP tool annotations on purpose, so an author moving a tool description into a Function Object keeps the same names. They are independent author assertions about the function's contract, not MCP server metadata carried through a call. Absent means unknown, not false. Policy engines MAY use them (for example, require approval for steps whose function lacks `readOnlyHint: true`) and MUST NOT treat them as guarantees.

### Binding Object

Common fields, flat, discriminated by `type`:

| Field | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `bindingId` | string | REQUIRED. Unique within its function, stable. The identity that policy and audit refer to, always qualified as (functionId, bindingId) |
| `type` | string | REQUIRED. `mcp` in this proposal; `x-` prefixed types allowed for experiments |

Profile fields sit at the top level of the binding (see the MCP profile below). No Binding Object field may contain a runtime expression in 1.2; bindings are static, and everything dynamic flows through `arguments`. Binding semantics are versioned by the `arazzo` version itself; if profiles later need to evolve independently, explicit profile versioning can be introduced then, with absence meaning the original 1.2 semantics. I would rather not ship version ceremony on day one.

An unknown `type` that is not `x-` prefixed makes the document invalid for 1.2. `x-` types are structurally valid and simply ineligible on executors that do not recognize them; their configuration lives in ordinary `x-` extension properties.

Closedness, stated once for everything: every object this proposal defines (Function, Binding, the step additions, `annotations`) is closed apart from `x-` specification extensions, which are permitted on all of them per Arazzo's existing extension convention. An unrecognized non-`x-` field is a document error. And because binding order is preference, tools that transform or re-serialize documents MUST preserve it.

### Step Object additions

| Field | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `functionId` | string | Names a Function Object in this document's top-level `functions` list |
| `arguments` | object | Argument construction, below |

Exactly one of `operationId`, `operationPath`, `channelPath`, `workflowId`, `functionId` MUST be present on a step, and `arguments` MUST NOT be present unless `functionId` is. A step's `functionId` MUST identify a Function Object defined in this document; a reference that does not resolve makes the document invalid. A function step MUST NOT use `parameters`, `requestBody`, `action`, or `correlationId`; those describe transports the function abstraction deliberately hides. For the same reason, the transport-scoped expression roots (`$statusCode`, `$response`, `$request`, `$message`) are invalid inside a function step's fields, whatever binding ends up selected. `timeout`, `dependsOn`, `successCriteria`, `onSuccess`/`onFailure`, and `outputs` keep their normal meaning.

Why `arguments` and not the existing `parameters`? Parameter identity in Arazzo is `(name, in)`, workflow-level parameters flow down into steps, and reusable parameter components exist. Every one of those interacts badly with a transport-free call: what would an inherited query parameter mean to a function? Rather than write a page of exceptions, function steps get a dedicated map with none of that history:

- Absent `arguments` means `{}`. The evaluated result is always a single JSON object, validated against `inputSchema` after evaluation, never before.
- Values may be literals, runtime expressions, or nested arrays and objects. Evaluation traverses arrays and objects recursively.
- A string value is treated as an expression only when the entire string matches the runtime-expression grammar; then it preserves the JSON type of whatever it resolves to (`query: $inputs.count` can produce a number). Expressions embedded inside longer strings use the existing `{}` convention and produce strings: `query: "ticket from {$inputs.reporterName}"`, and a braced whole string like `"{$inputs.count}"` is therefore a string too.
- A `$`-prefixed string that does not match the grammar (`"$100"`) is an ordinary literal. An escape convention for text that legitimately looks like an embedding is a PR-stage detail.
- Workflow-level `parameters` are never inherited by function steps.

## Document conformance vs execution readiness

This distinction does the most work in the whole proposal, so here it is precisely. Three phases:

1. Document conformance: structural and semantic validity of the document itself. Environment-independent. The same document is valid or invalid everywhere.
2. Execution preparation: a specific executor, with its configuration, capabilities, and policy, resolves symbolic targets and selects a binding for every function reachable from the workflow it was asked to run. All selection happens here.
3. Invocation: steps execute against the frozen selections.

Reachable is defined statically: the transitive closure starting at the invoked workflow, covering every `functionId` referenced by its steps plus everything reached through `workflowId` step targets and through workflows named by `goto`/`retry` failure actions. When a `workflowId` target lives in another arazzo document, that document's reachable functions prepare under the same snapshot.

| Situation | Conformance | Readiness |
|---|---|---|
| Binding with unknown non-`x-` `type` | invalid document | n/a |
| Step references a `functionId` not defined in the document | invalid document | n/a |
| Binding with recognized `type` the executor does not support | valid | binding ineligible |
| Binding with `x-` `type` | valid | ineligible unless explicitly supported |
| Referenced function ends up with no eligible binding | valid | preparation fails before any step executes |
| Function defined but not reachable from the workflow being run | valid | no readiness requirement |

So a document that binds a function only through some `x-vendor-queue` binding is a valid Arazzo document everywhere and lints everywhere, and it executes only where that binding is supported. Validity is universal, runnability is environmental, and the failure mode for un-runnable is a preparation-time diagnostic naming the function, never a surprise at step 7.

Non-executing tools (linters, editors, doc generators) validate document conformance and are done. They SHOULD report "this function has no binding I recognize" at information severity, not as an error, and tools that display a multi-binding function SHOULD present the bindings as environment-resolved alternatives, not as step-level control flow.

### Binding selection

Selection is per prepared execution, not per document load, since a loaded document may be shared across tenants or principals:

1. Take a fixed snapshot of capabilities, configuration, policy, and security context.
2. Resolve profile-defined symbolic identities (for example `serverName`) from configuration.
3. Remove bindings that are unsupported, unresolvable, or policy-prohibited.
4. If policy pins a specific binding, identified as a (functionId, bindingId) pair, that binding must be eligible, otherwise preparation fails.
5. Otherwise select the first eligible binding in document order.
6. Freeze the triple (function identity, `bindingId`, resolved target identity) for the execution, including all retries of the step. Each profile defines what its resolved target identity is.
7. Invocation failure, authorization revocation, or target liveness failure never causes reselection.

Policy may filter and may pin. It may not "prefer" one binding over another without a deterministic rule; preference ordering is the author's job, expressed by the order of the `bindings` array. Retries retry the selected binding or fail. Falling back to a different binding mid-run would mean a workflow silently changes transport and privilege on failure, which is how surprising incidents get written.

One narrow carve-out for durable executions: a run that suspends (paused for approval, resumed days later) MAY re-resolve the selected binding's symbolic target under a fresh snapshot at the resume boundary, recording that re-resolution in its audit trail. The selection itself, the `bindingId`, never changes. Credentials rotate and fleets move; bindings do not.

## Results and errors

A function step introduces two expression roots:

- `$result`: the normalized function result, a JSON value validated against `outputSchema`.
- `$error`: a structured error, present only when the invocation failed.

Both are usable bare (the whole value) or with a `#` JSON Pointer fragment (`$result#/userId`, `$error#/code`), the same fragment convention `$response.body` carries today; the exact ABNF additions land with the PR, and these are the only two access forms. They are valid only in fields evaluated in the function step's own context: its `successCriteria`, its `outputs`, and the criteria of its `onSuccess`/`onFailure` actions (including reusable actions, when referenced from a function step). Anywhere else is a document error where that is statically detectable, and an evaluation failure otherwise. Later steps read the values through declared outputs (`$steps.who.outputs.userId`), same as everything else in Arazzo.

| Outcome | `$result` | `$error` |
|---|---|---|
| Invocation succeeds, output valid | present | absent |
| Invocation succeeds, `successCriteria` fails | present | absent |
| Output fails `outputSchema` | absent | present (`schema`, code `output-schema`) |
| Invocation fails | absent | present |
| Preparation failure | step never runs | step never runs |

A criteria failure is not a function error; failure actions can inspect `$result` to decide what to do. When `outputSchema` validation fails there is no partial `$result`: exposing a value the document just declared invalid would put criteria in the position of consuming data the contract rejected. In criteria, referencing a root that is absent for the outcome at hand (say, `$error` after a success) evaluates to false rather than failing evaluation, so mixed handlers stay writable; in `outputs`, referencing an absent root is an evaluation failure. Across retries, `$error` reflects the most recent attempt, and a retry that succeeds clears it.

`$error` fields:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `type` | one of `timeout`, `transport`, `protocol`, `application`, `schema`, `policy` |
| `code` | short stable string. Portable only where this spec or a profile pins its value; branch on `type` otherwise |
| `message` | human-readable diagnostic; non-portable, do not branch on it |

There is deliberately no structured payload field on `$error` in this proposal; a profile that needs to expose machine-readable error bodies can propose one later.

The types:

- `timeout`: the step deadline expired.
- `transport`: the exchange could not be completed (connect, TLS, channel loss).
- `protocol`: the exchange completed but was malformed for the profile (JSON-RPC error, result codec violation).
- `application`: the target ran and reported failure (MCP `isError`).
- `schema`: input or output contract validation failed. Pinned codes: `input-schema` and `output-schema`.
- `policy`: the executor refused the invocation at invocation time, for example an egress rule tripped by a resolved target or a credential broker refusing the call.

An example, since `code` is the branching mechanism: an `onFailure` criterion can read `$error#/type == "timeout"` or, under the MCP profile below, `$error#/code == "tool-error"`.

Boundary cases, stated so implementations do not have to guess:

- Preparation-time policy denial is a preparation diagnostic, not `$error`. No step ran.
- A failure to evaluate an `arguments` expression is an ordinary Arazzo expression evaluation failure, the same as anywhere else in a document. `$error` covers function invocation outcomes, not every possible step failure (whether evaluation errors deserve their own structured surface is open question 3, and it would be Arazzo-wide).
- Workflow cancellation is control flow, not `timeout`, and produces no `$error`.
- Note, informative: `timeout` and `transport` do not prove the call had no side effects. Retry and compensation logic must assume outcome-unknown, which is also part of why `idempotentHint` exists.

Timeouts: the existing step `timeout` is the end-to-end deadline for the function invocation, each profile defines cancellation and cleanup at expiry, and no new timeout field is added. An executor MAY impose a shorter effective deadline by policy; when its ceiling fires, that surfaces as `timeout` too.

## Profile: MCP (Streamable HTTP)

| Field | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `serverName` | string | symbolic server identity, resolved from executor configuration by exact, case-sensitive match. Exactly one of `serverName`, `url` |
| `url` | string | explicit MCP endpoint |
| `tool` | string | REQUIRED. The MCP tool name |
| `resultMode` | string | optional; one of the four codecs below. Absent means `structuredContent` |

Invocation is `tools/call` with the evaluated arguments object, over normal MCP session establishment and version negotiation. Credentials attach to the resolved target through executor configuration, never through the document; a target with no resolvable credentials is unresolvable at selection step 3. The profile's resolved target identity, the thing selection step 6 freezes, is the configuration-resolved logical target for the `serverName` form and the literal endpoint for the `url` form.

The result codec is explicit because MCP results are a content array, and "take the first text block" is lossy and non-portable:

- `structuredContent`: require `structuredContent` on the result and return it.
- `content`: return the complete MCP content array as the result value.
- `jsonText`: require exactly one text block containing exactly one JSON value; return that value.
- `text`: require exactly one text block; return it as a JSON string.

Anything ambiguous or incompatible with the declared mode is a `protocol` error. Nothing is silently discarded.

Error mapping, with pinned codes so criteria can branch portably: a tool result carrying `isError: true` is `application` with code `tool-error`. A JSON-RPC level error is `protocol` with the JSON-RPC error code as a decimal string; a result codec violation is `protocol` with code `result-codec`. Connection and TLS failures are `transport` (codes implementation-defined; branch on `type`).

Cancellation: when the step deadline expires, the executor sends the MCP cancellation notification for the in-flight request, discards any result that arrives afterward (a result racing the deadline is discarded, never returned), and surfaces `timeout`. Whether the session survives is environmental.

## Security

A document format should say what documents mean, not how executors run things. So, three statements about meaning:

- Nothing in a document grants authority. What an invocation may actually do is derived from the resolved target, executor configuration, expanded argument values, ambient credentials, and operator policy; a document can narrow expectations, never widen permissions, and annotations are policy hints, never enforcement.
- A document can cause network access through configured targets, literal endpoints, and redirects. None of it is exempt from the environment's egress policy; the document never gets to vouch for a destination.
- Credential handling is profile-defined and environmental. Documents never carry secrets.

## Conformance

Independent conformance targets, so a vendor can claim exactly what they implement:

- Function Core: document validation, selection semantics, `$result` and `$error`, preparation behavior.
- MCP profile.

An executor does not have to support the profile, and a validation-only tool can claim Function Core alone. The profile is in this issue because a core with zero concrete profiles is not reviewable, not because supporting it is mandatory. Packaging, not coupling.

Conformance fixtures should live in this repository next to the proposal, with machine-checkable expectations; they are how rule zero stops being a slogan. The shape I have in mind, for "recognized-but-unsupported fails preparation, not validation":

```yaml
# fixture fn-prep-001
given:
  profiles: [mcp]
  resolvable: {}
document:
  arazzo: 1.2.0
  info: {title: fn-prep-001, version: 1.0.0}
  functions:
    - functionId: notHere
      inputSchema: {type: object}
      outputSchema: {type: object}
      bindings:
        - {bindingId: exp, type: x-vendor-queue}
  workflows:
    - workflowId: w1
      steps:
        - stepId: s1
          functionId: notHere
expect:
  documentValidation: pass
  executionPreparation:
    outcome: reject
    reason: no-eligible-binding
    functionId: notHere
  stepsExecuted: 0
```

The `given` block is what makes the fixture portable: it declares the environment (supported profiles, resolvable symbolic names, policy pins) so two vendors run the same test, not two tests that happen to share a document. Illustrative here; the PR-stage spec text enumerates the closed vocabulary of `outcome` and `reason` values, defines `stepsExecuted` as the count of steps that entered invocation (retries counted once), and adds the other fixture classes: validation-fail fixtures carrying an expected error location, selection fixtures asserting the chosen (functionId, bindingId) pair, and execution fixtures asserting per-binding invocation counts, which is what makes the no-fallback rule testable rather than taken on faith.

## Out of scope, deliberately

- Function registries and discovery. Documents are self-contained; where functions come from is a tooling topic.
- Inline function definitions on steps. Deferred. A function defined once at the top level and referenced by id keeps identity simple, and inline can be added later without breaking anything.
- Cross-document function reuse through source descriptions. Deferred for the same reason.
- Binding profiles for local processes (`cli`, MCP over stdio). The profile half would be legitimate spec territory: how arguments become argv and stdin, how exit codes and streams map to `$result` and `$error`. How an executor isolates, authorizes, or resource-limits a local process is not, and this proposal does not try to say. If there is appetite, local bindings can be their own proposal; nothing in Function Core depends on them.
- A bare-HTTP profile. I drafted one and split it out before posting; see open question 1.
- A WebAssembly profile. Wasm belongs in the motivation, but a real profile needs normative ABI decisions (component model version, interface shape, WASI expectations, resource limits) that deserve their own proposal. Until then `wasm` is simply not in the closed type set, so the existing unknown-type rule already keeps it out of 1.2 documents, and experiments can use an `x-` binding.
- Non-JSON contract payloads, streaming, and partial results.

## Open questions

1. Bare HTTP endpoints with no published description. I drafted a narrow JSON-only `http` profile and cut it before posting: the honest counter-argument is that a minimal OpenAPI description plus `operationId` already covers that case. Is a bare-HTTP profile worth a follow-up proposal, or is "describe it" the answer?
2. Abstract functions: a contract with no bindings, resolved by an out-of-band overlay. Rejected for 1.2 because it reintroduces the unspecified-convention problem, but a standardized overlay or registry mechanism could make it sound later, and nothing here blocks that.
3. Should structured evaluation errors (for `arguments` and everywhere else expressions appear) become an Arazzo-wide facility some day? I intentionally kept `$error` away from them.
4. Is authoring responsibility the right framing for multi-binding behavioral equivalence, or does the group want stronger language?

## Relation to #410

#410 is the umbrella. This is the first piece split out of it, and the one worth pinning down first because the rest layers on top. Further binding profiles (bare HTTP, local processes, wasm) can follow as their own proposals if the group wants them.

If you read this far: tear it apart. The proposal gets better the more of it fails review.
